methodology.title: Curated source-first AI intelligence brief
methodology.summary: This dataset is generated from public source feeds. Items are linked back to their original URLs, timestamped, and auto-categorized for triage rather than treated as infallible truth.
caveats: Feed freshness depends on source publication latency and RSS availability.
Threads coverage uses RSSHub adapters and may fail or lag if the upstream route changes.
Automatic categorization is heuristic and should be reviewed for decision-critical workflows.

research.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
research.summary: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

research.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
research.summary: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

research.title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
research.summary: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.

research.title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
research.summary: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

research.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
research.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

research.title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
research.summary: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

research.title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
research.summary: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).

research.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
research.summary: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

research.title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
research.summary: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

research.title: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
research.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.

research.title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
research.summary: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.

research.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
research.summary: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

news.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
news.summary: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.  Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper , the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.  However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.  For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.  These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.  With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.  Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.
